title: Sam Altman’s underrated AI fear: that we stop thinking for ourselves
excerpt: The man whose company is trying to get the world to use AI for everything has named a risk he thinks almost no one is talking about: that people will let it do so much of their thinking that their own minds go slack. Sam Altman, OpenAI’s
content_html:
The man whose company is trying to get the world to use AI for everything has named a risk he thinks almost no one is talking about: that people will let it do so much of their thinking that their own minds go slack.

Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, calls it “cognitive atrophy,” and puts it near the top of AI’s unresolved questions. He said it on the podcast “Invest Like the Best.”

Asked what most worried him about AI’s future, Altman replied: “One that I don’t think gets much attention is how are we going to avoid cognitive atrophy?”

His framing was less doom than discipline. “How are we going to use these tools and make sure that we are stretching our brains more and more and continuing to understand the stuff that really matters?” he asked, casting the danger as one of laziness rather than apocalypse.

It is a striking worry coming from him. OpenAI’s whole business is persuading people to lean on ChatGPT for more of their work and their decisions, which makes its founder fretting about over-reliance a little like a confectioner warning about sugar.

The research is starting to back the worry. Nataliya Kosmyna, an MIT researcher, ran a preliminary study in which people who used generative AI to write essays performed worse over time than those who used Google or no help at all.

Her framing was blunt. “There’s never been a tool like this that has offered us the opportunity to let thinking be done for us.”

Others put the risk in starker terms. Vivienne Ming, a theoretical neuroscientist, calls the habit of handing cognitive work to AI “chronic substitution,” and warns that repeating it could erode the cognitive reserve that helps defend the brain against dementia.

The concern sharpens as AI takes on more. The tools have moved beyond answering questions to doing document review, research, analysis, customer support, and coding, which means the mental work being offloaded is no longer trivial.

Altman is not the first tech boss to say so. Last year Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French lab Mistral, told The Times that AI’s biggest risk might be “deskilling” workers and making them progressively lazier as they lean on it to think.

The pattern is old, only sharper. Calculators, satnav, and search each took over a skill people used to keep in their heads, and each drew the same warning, usually without the collapse the warnings predicted.

What is different now is breadth. Earlier tools offloaded one narrow task; a general-purpose assistant can read, write, reason, and decide, which makes the question of what humans keep practising a far larger one.

Altman, for his part, did not stay gloomy. He described a “pretty magical” future in which an always-on personal AI reads your documents, listens to your meetings, recalls emails from weeks ago, and uses spare overnight computing power to generate ideas and tell you what to do next.

Even so, he drew a line around what the machines cannot do. “The world may need like a new kind of word for the kind of judgment that people are very good at, that AI seems to really deeply struggle with,” Altman said, a rare admission of the tool’s limits from its chief salesman.

That is the tension he is living. Altman can believe both that AI will make people more capable and that it might make them lazier, and OpenAI is pushing the tool into ever more of daily life while its founder warns about exactly that.

The honest answer is that no one knows yet. Whether AI stretches our brains or lets them soften depends on how people use it, and Altman, who has worried before about his own inability to put down a screen, is not promising the good outcome, only naming the risk.

content_html_zh:
这位公司试图让世界在一切事物上使用人工智能的人指出了一个他认为几乎没有人谈论的风险：人们会让人工智能完成他们的大部分思考，以至于他们自己的思维变得松弛。

OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼 (Sam Altman) 将其称为“认知萎缩”，并将其列为人工智能未解决问题的首要问题。 他在播客“像最好的那样投资”中说道。

当被问及他对人工智能的未来最担心的是什么时，奥尔特曼回答说：“我认为没有引起太多关注的是我们如何避免认知萎缩？”

他的框架与其说是厄运，不如说是纪律。 “我们如何使用这些工具并确保我们越来越多地拓展我们的大脑并继续理解真正重要的东西？” 他问道，将这种危险视为一种懒惰而不是世界末日。

他的担忧令人震惊。 OpenAI 的整个业务是说服人们在更多的工作和决策中依赖 ChatGPT，这使得其创始人对过度依赖的担忧有点像糖果商对糖的警告。

这项研究开始证实了这种担忧。 麻省理工学院研究员 Nataliya Kosmyna 进行了一项初步研究，结果显示，随着时间的推移，使用生成式人工智能来撰写论文的人比那些使用谷歌或根本不使用任何帮助的人表现更差。

她的框架很生硬。 “从来没有像这样的工具为我们提供了让我们思考的机会。”

其他人则用更严厉的措辞来描述这种风险。 理论神经科学家薇薇安·明 (Vivienne Ming) 将把认知工作交给人工智能的习惯称为“慢性替代”，并警告说，重复这种做法可能会削弱有助于大脑抵御痴呆症的认知储备。

随着人工智能发挥的作用越来越大，人们的担忧也越来越严重。 这些工具已经不再只是回答问题，而是进行文档审查、研究、分析、客户支持和编码，这意味着卸下的脑力工作不再是微不足道的。

奥特曼并不是第一个这么说的科技老板。 去年，法国米斯特拉尔实验室首席执行官阿瑟·门施 (Arthur Mensch) 告诉《泰晤士报》，人工智能最大的风险可能是“降低”工人的技能，让他们在依赖人工智能进行思考时变得越来越懒。

图案很旧，只是更清晰。 计算器、卫星导航和搜索都取代了人们过去牢记在心的一项技能，并且都发出了相同的警告，通常不会出现警告所预测的崩溃。

现在不同的是广度。 早期的工具只承担了一项狭窄的任务；通用助理可以阅读、写作、推理和决策，这使得人类不断练习什么的问题变得更加重要。

就奥特曼而言，他并没有保持悲观。 他描述了一个“非常神奇”的未来，在这个未来中，永远在线的个人人工智能会读取你的文档、听取你的会议、回忆几周前的电子邮件，并利用夜间闲置的计算能力来产生想法并告诉你下一步该做什么。

即便如此，他还是对机器不能做的事情划定了界限。 奥特曼表示：“世界可能需要一个新的词来形容人们非常擅长的判断，而人工智能似乎确实在与这种判断作斗争。”他的首席推销员罕见地承认了该工具的局限性。

这就是他所承受的压力。 Altman 相信人工智能会让人们变得更有能力，也可能会让他们变得更加懒惰，而 OpenAI 正在将这种工具推向日常生活，而其创始人恰恰对此发出了警告。

诚实的答案是，目前还没有人知道。 人工智能是让我们的大脑发挥作用还是让大脑变软，取决于人们如何使用它，而此前曾担心自己无法放下屏幕的奥特曼并没有承诺好的结果，只是指出了风险。
